I thank the minister for his statement, and particularly his complimentary remarks with regard to the former minister. It has come to my attention that there has been a great need for this department. As we all know, it was established by the former government and I greatly appreciate the minister's remarks, particularly the complimentary way in which he spoke of the former minister. We all feel much the same. I say sincerely to the minister that I hope he will enjoy a similar association with this department.
I want to bring to the minister's attention this afternoon some aspects of forestry management, particularly as they relate to what is known as the eastern Rockies watershed. This area is important not only to my constituency but to the prairie provinces as a whole. I find some difficulty, Mr. Chairman, in separating the actual management and conservation of forests from water and soil conservation and the production that is so closely related thereto. However, in discussing forest conservation and production I have to bear in mind, as I said before, the relationship of the conservation of our water supply.
I have in mind an example or two to which I should like to call the minister's attention as well as the attention of the members of the department. The need is very urgent at the moment, and the sooner something can be done about this the better it will be for the whole country. I am referring to the recent floods we have had in this area. Practically everyone in this house has had his attention drawn to the floods that occurred on the eastern watershed of the Rockies, particularly in the southern area where most of the damage was done. Those floods were not entirely the result of an act of God but resulted from what I might almost term mismanagement. I do not choose to use that word at this stage, but there are one or two things that should be brought to the attention of the department and of people in general. It is something we have to be aware of and,
Supply-Forestry
as a matter of fact, should be aware of before it happens. That is the way real conservation and production are reached, to recognize the needs before things like this happen.
I may be just a little bit out of order, Mr. Chairman, but I wish to point out two examples, one of them being something that happened in a national park and the other adjacent to it on the eastern slopes of the Rockies. I believe it would be well for the minister and his officials to consider closer co-operation with the parks department because the first example I mention deals with an area of mature timber. A strong wind went through it and levelled this timber which, a few years previously, had been in its prime and, if handled properly, would not only have benefited the park and the people who visit it, but the country as a whole. Now, however, this watershed is completely waste.
With proper co-operation between the departments this could have been avoided, thus aiding the beautification of the park, the utilization of valuable forest products and the preservation of the watershed to maintain supplies of water for the adjacent areas.
I mention this example because the minister said he wanted advice. I do not purport to present this as advice. I do not pretend to be advising the minister, but things like this require urgent action and they are happening all over the country. The other day I visited in Ontario and a few weeks before that in Quebec, and in both places I saw the results of forest mismanagement in depletion of the soil and water supplies. If I may digress for a moment, there is one very real example of this in the reduced water levels of the great lakes and in the St. Lawrence seaway. The low levels in the St. Lawrence seaway have actually affected the delivery of western grain and other products. Boats are not able to load to their full capacities, which results in higher freight costs and stiffer competition for export trade.
The other example I want to mention is related very closely to forest management. I believe the departmental officials should co-operate with provincial authorities on the practice of allowing livestock to be pastured in forest areas. Some areas have been badly damaged by over-grazing in the summer months. They are very valuable sources of pasture for livestock producers and could become much more valuable, but the sorry fact is that some of them have been abused and neglected. This is something which is closely related to forest conservation and

Supply-Forestry
Canadian production as a whole, and if matters like this are neglected or ignored they can tend to deplete our water supplies.
In my area some people think we will never run short of water, which is used in three main ways, namely for irrigation-we have half a million acres under irrigation- for commercial demands, and for domestic uses. Other people however are beginning to wonder which use has a prior right. A few years of drought and, through neglect, a forest fire, would result in a reduction of the water supply. What would happen then when the three prime users would begin to vie and compete with each other for the existing supply?
The very fact that this department was created a few years ago has brought home more than ever to the Canadian people the great need for conservation, and I like to relate this to production, because through proper management we can aid the production of forest products and agricultural products and at the same time conserve our water supplies. I would like to relate this need for conservation to the ARDA program but I understand we will be doing this a little later and that other speakers will mention it. I think the ARDA program is a good one but I believe it has not been applied as rapidly and as usefully as it should. Related to forest production and conservation, it is a wonderful program. I complimented the minister earlier. I am quite sure he will take a very active interest in this matter, and before long I hope these two programs will dovetail and not only increase our production but our potential in this connection.
I also wanted to say something with regard to ARDA, soil and water conservation and the management and production thereof. I also have a word or two to say about feed grains. I will not say very much about these matters at this time except to mention that I am extremely interested in them and will be looking forward to hearing other hon. members putting forward their points of view this afternoon. This all ties in, Mr. Chairman; it is so hard to separate conservation from production. Forest conservation and production, water conservation, land conservation and their production are all tied together.
I shall conclude my remarks now, Mr. Chairman, and urge the minister very sincerely to keep these few suggestions in mind. I would also say that we on this side of the house, in spite of some of the things that take place now and then, are very sincerely interested in these matters and would be glad

to co-operate with the minister and his department on any and every opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot dissemble my disappointment at the introductory remarks of the minister. I will not say he was beating around the bush, but he reminded me very much of a former minister of this house, Henri Courtemanche, when he presented his first estimates. There was that diffident approach of, "I have only been here a few months", sort of thing, "and I haven't really got a grip on things. But you just wait. One of these days I am going to be there". I would like to point out to the minister that he entered upon his portfolio with a considerable reputation, a reputation that I think a great many of us respect; that of a man of energy, education and imagination. He has been given the responsibility of a portfolio that has a great opportunity. Yet here, when he introduces his estimates, we get in effect the old, traditional lead-off speech by a minister who is in charge of nothing more than a bureaucracy, tossing off a few statistics, a few remarks and a brief outline of the organization that has been prepared for him by his deputy.
I suggest to the minister that this kind of introduction is not what we expected from him and I do not think it is up to his capacities and abilities. I suggest he has a magnificent opportunity with this department, and so far he has not given any indication that he is going to seize it. I am not talking about feed grains and eastern agriculture; I am talking about forestry. I want to give credit to members who are no longer with us, having been defeated in elections. I refer to the then members for Nanaimo, for Comox-Alberni, Mr. McQuillan, and for Coast-Capilano, who are no longer with us. They shared with me the task of writing a committee report several years ago following many meetings of the committee on mines, forests and waters, which in many ways led to the creation of the Department of Forestry. I would also like to compliment the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who it seems to me was the man in the cabinet at the time who had the perspective as to what this department might be.
The vision.

I was bitterly disappointed- and I have expressed it in this house before-over the fact that the first minister and the one who followed him were in a sense carrying on what were nothing more than the traditions that had been established by rather

effective but limited branches dealing with forestry; I am thinking particularly of the forestry branch and the forest products research organization. I have nothing critical to say, but if the minister would go back and look at the recommendations that came out of that committee he would realize we had a much wider and greater dream, or vision, if you want, for a federal Department of Forestry. He has not given any indication that he has anything of that sort in mind.
I suggest to the minister that he may be confounded over the fact that he is an ambitious person within the political framework and may be seeing his role more as a politician than as the imaginative leader of a department. I suggest that the way for him to move to a really senior place in our political situation is to really do something with this department. I believe that nothing has really been achieved yet by the Department of Forestry. As a matter of fact, if I could make the recommendation now or have any influence on it, after taking a continued interest in forestry and being one of those who wanted the department set up, I would say we might as well go back to the old situation, stick the forest products branch and the forestry branch back in the department from which they came, and look to the Department of Industry for the kind of imaginative development in forestry on the economic and industrial side that we would want.
As hon. members may be aware, I represent the largest constituency in Ontario. Its whole base is in the forest industry. It is perhaps the most productive part of Ontario, in dollar terms, where forestry is concerned. The regional, Port Arthur branch of the provincial department of lands and forests is probably the most important one in Ontario. In other words, the lakehead plays somewhat the same part and holds the same position in the pulp and paper and forestry industry in Ontario as the community of Three Rivers traditionally plays in the province of Quebec. Because of this basic economic factor, anyone who represents the area has to be concerned with and involved in forestry matters.
As a result of this I have spent a considerable time looking at American installations in the lake states; I have paid a visit to Finland and Russia to look at some of their forestry methods and the way they do things; I have had contact, as someone who established a forestry research library, at least with the literature on the subject; and I am very much aware-at least, this is my opinion -that we desperately need some kind of
Supply-Forestry
breakthrough in leadership on the federal scene in order to achieve the kind of solutions to our forestry problems which have not yet been forthcoming.
I would like to suggest to the minister some of the ways in which he should move and some of the reasons for the difficulties. I think one of the prime reasons for the difficulties in forestry relates to the very success of the forest industry itself; I am thinking particularly of the pulp and paper industry. I think the position was put in a nutshell by perhaps the most famous of all Canadian foresters, certainly the wealthiest, namely H. R. MacMillan. In 1957 H. R. MacMillan, with 50 years of professional experience behind him, said:
It is doubtful whether Canada, with its present attention to forest management, can sustain today's annual cut in perpetuity, even by going farther north each decade into virgin forest (at greater cost for logs) or by using a higher proportion of inferior species (thus reducing our competitive ability in the foreign markets on which we depend).
I know of very little since 1957 which has changed that basic situation which H. R. MacMillan pointed out. One of the real tragedies is this. When I raised this matter in the house once before, one of the senior people in the forestry field in Ontario belaboured me in the forestry newsletter; but I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that one of the prime difficulties is the very success of the forest industry, which in its pulp and paper aspect has given the actual foresters as a profession really no choice at all. I think forestry is more than a science; to a considerable extent it is an art. But a forester has to take a very long view because he is dealing with something that moves in cycles. A decade means nothing when you are managing a forest. The very approach of the forester, with his long range view and concern for the whole climate and the ecology of materials, and the large corporation with its annual report and quarterly dividends, tends to pull things asunder.
One of the unfortunate things is that foresters, as persons professionally trained and dedicated to an ideal, have not made their way with great speed up the ladder in the country's industries. It is much more often the chartered accountant who becomes the big wheel, or the logging superintendent with an engineering background, and one of the consequences is that all too rarely in our forest industry do we have that kind of idealistic conception. A forester, I would put to you, does deal with an ideal. It is the ideal of the perfect forest with the best possible use being made of it. You cannot live in a Utopia

Supply-Forestry
and you cannot create a Utopia, but it seems to me that it should always be an ideal; and it should always be the ideal in forestry to have the kind of conservation in silviculture which is always considering the forest at its best and optimum use, and getting the most commercial use from it.
In Finland I was impressed with the way both private and public forestry has entered the country and enabled it to get a fantastic return from its forests. I would point out to hon. members that Finland is a country approximately the same area as my constituency with approximately the same amount of forest cover. In many ways we have a better soil and climate than Finland has. Perhaps we do not have quite as long a growing season but there is quite a similarity. Yet Finland, a country with four to five million people, is able to accomplish a tremendous amount in paying back reparation, in supporting one of the best and most attractive small countries in Europe largely on its forests. Those forests represent an area no more than what we have in my riding of Port Arthur in terms of square miles. Dr. Piha, head of Finnish forestry, when I told him I was so impressed with their practices in Finland, said to me: "I am afraid you do not get good forestry practices till there is a desperate shortage of wood; till people begin to realize that there is no alternative to good forest management. We had to wait for it in Finland". He said the same thing followed from his Swedish experience.
Then I asked him what the Russians were doing, and he said that they have so much forest land they are just biting into it and really do not know where they are going. I had the pleasure of going to Leningrad and talking to forestry specialists there, and I think his judgment was correct. The Russians do have so much by way of forested land that they really have not got a good preliminary survey under way yet and they are not sure as to their future. But they have a logging and management concept which I think is tremendously advanced. They have plans for their cut-over areas which are much ahead of anything I know or which has been conceived of in this country, particularly by the provinces.
I make these points, Mr. Chairman, about what I saw in Finland and Russia really to come to my conclusion, that I do not think the experience of any other countries can be at all translated. I did not come back from there with the feeling that there were great lessons to be learned from either Finland or

Russia on the part of Canadian foresters. I am sure that some of our logging people could get ideas in the way of mass producing and whole tree logging, but I do not think you can apply experience of other countries to the kind of traditions and experiences which we have. However, I do think it is worth while going to see what other people such as the Finns and the Swedes can achieve by way of greater use of forest resources which are much greater than we have, and this is all tied in with a total use concept, which includes recreation, boating, camping, and living in the forest, things we have not even thought of or reached for yet.
Our problems in this country really come down to the fact that we have 11 different forest policies. Given 11 different forest policies, what role has the federal government in forestry? I can only put it in simple terms, Mr. Chairman: We have no role at all. I think it has been something of a charlatan here with regard to what we have been allowed to develop in terms of federal forest agencies, because these agencies really cannot play a positive role at the present time. They go through the motions, and they are rather good motions, of the forest roads program, the reforestation program, support for forest fire protection, a bit of general collusion on information, and some good research in forest products. But there is a tremendous limitation on it because of the variety of jurisdictions of operation, because of the jealousies which are in existence and because the forestry profession in Canada itself is not sure where it is going or what it needs to be doing.
I suggest to the minister that there are at least three places where he can look for and find opportunities to enlarge the scope of the Department of Forestry and to enable it not only to give leadership but begin to wipe out some of the varieties of standards which we possess. I want to start with what is the simplest one, and in a sense the least far-reaching. This is a suggestion I put to the former minister of forestry, who is sitting in the house now, but I never heard any more from him. I told him that he should be the first minister of forestry to realize that the best way to solve our Indian problem in this country is to tie in a real forestry development program with the Indians, who in most parts of the country live in forested areas, so that the Indian has some kind of economic confidence and is able to work in the forest. At the present time there is hardly a reserve in the country with a decent forest stand. I

suggest that a lot of things could be renegotiated with the provincial governments. At least, they are now paying lipservice through their departments of lands and forests to doing something for the Indians.
Forestry work, whether it is planting trees for a couple of weeks in the spring or fall or whether it is actually doing logging work, is something which the Indians can get on to. It is a natural for the kind of community in which they are used to living. But there must be much more leadership coming from the Indian affairs branch in this particular regard. Several years ago I tried to set up a project on forestry work for Indians in a reserve near lake Nipigon and I wound up with an involvement of four different private organizations which held leases from the provincial department, and also the trade unions became involved. So this is the complicating factor: The forests of Canada are being exploited at the present time within the private management framework and the trade union framework. It is going to take a tremendous amount of development work and initiative, and the sort of expenditure that the federal government might provide, before we are able to make a breakthrough and employ Indians to work as trained technicians, or loggers, or people carrying out the most routine and simple kind of silviculture improvement work.
It is my suggestion that this is one of the things which the Minister of Forestry can do in the country, but it will not be done by sitting in an office in Ottawa listening to officials who are used to a bureaucratic approach for all their generation. It will not be any good going to the Indian affairs branch and talking to their officials, who think in terms of rations and some kind of handout program, of $500 here or $1,000 there, or letting them cut cordwood for the winter to keep their houses warm. It must be something which both the government and the minister throw themselves into. I suggest that this is one field which would take the Department of Forestry into almost every province in the country and give it and its officials and the professional people a much greater understanding of some of the problems met by the local communities.
I mention this because so often when I talk with foresters and loggers in the industry I encounter a kind of pleasant contempt which they have for the federal Department of Forestry. I do not go along with their contempt, but their attitude is usually based in
Supply-Forestry
dollars and cents terms. They feel if something pays, it is worth while, but that these fellows spend too much of their time in Ottawa and Petawawa, and forestry stations, frigging around with experiments. This department has sample plots all over the country, and what good are they? I understand if one could put the sample plots that have been established in this country end to end, in order to visit them all a man would have to go across Canada and back. As a matter of fact, I imagine a good deal of the foresters spend much of their time trying to make sure they have not lost track of all the records in respect of the sample plots. Perhaps I am exaggerating somewhat, but in many ways that is the situation.
I believe that if some of our professional foresters in the federal service were really at work bringing the Indians into a program associated with forestry, lumbering and logging, which was practical and really trained them, we would really begin to move the Indians off the reservations and provide the type of income that would do something for them. I should like to point out to the minister that I have on occasion witnessed an Indian who got out and worked for a pulp and paper company and eventually earned $6,000 or $7,000 per year. If one really wishes to consider the materialism aspect of this situation, he has only to look at that kind of Indian who is earning a good income, which captures him, so that he begins to move up in social class terms. This may sound crude, but this is the kind of thing we need for the Indians in order to give them the kind of income and economic future that will enable them to share in the material things we have and provide educational opportunities for their children. The Indian is not going to do this as long as he is sequestered on a reserve, living on the rations, handouts and paternalism that he now receives from the Indian affairs branch.
The Indian affairs branch was very pleased last year because in my area they found the opportunity of appointing an officer to look after the educational and employment opportunities for Indians in northwestern Ontario. He is looking after the employment and educational opportunities for about 16,000 Indians scattered 800 miles east and west and 500 miles north and south. What kind of an impact do you expect to make in respect of creating employment opportunities for Indians with that point of view?
I suggest to the minister that the first step he must take as the Minister of Forestry to really achieve the kind of reputation he would

Supply-Forestry
like for his department is in the direction of using the forestry industry as a means of making the Indians in our country full time citizens with economic opportunities. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, the minister will not have an easy job in this regard. The situation will vary from place to place in the country, and a successful approach will require a tremendous amount of diplomacy, having regard to trade unions in particular, and provincial departments. I think the people in Canada have good will and intentions in this respect.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal now with the second point I wish to draw to the minister's attention. When I was rather young I travelled a good deal in northern Minnesota and was rather impressed by the example set by the United States civilian conservation corps. During the depression years the civilian conservation corps employed 3,000 boys and young men during the first year it was organized and 5,000 in its second year. This is the kind of undertaking we need to deal with the growing problems with which we are faced. We would be required to follow this example on a smaller scale, of course, but through such an organization I certainly can see the possibility of both a meaningful conservation program developing, about which so many foresters love to talk at conventions-and that is about all-as well as some useful conservation being carried out by young people. This program could also include the planning and developing of parks.
It seems to me we have built a raft of schools all over this country under the vocational and technical assistance act. We have spent an astronomical amount, approximately $500 million. I think within two or three years this program will cost the federal government almost $1 billion. This is a good program, and certainly provides training schools in many parts of the country, but the basic industry relies upon forests, which in many ways have been disappearing. One can talk a good deal about sustained yield, but approximately 35 per cent of the cut-overs in the pulp and paper country of Ontario and Quebec are really not regenerated to any degree of quality. Considering the kind of personnel we have, water pollution, low water levels, the demand and response in respect of the parks we have created, I feel a civilian conservation corps could play a tremendous role in this country. Such a program would tie in perfectly with the kind of

practical education opportunities we wish to provide a great many people.
In Ontario there is a junior forest rangers scheme in operation. Young lads are put to work during their summer holidays, but there are almost ten times as many boys who want this opportunity as there are opportunities provided by the department of lands and forests. The greatest demand for this kind of opportunity exists in the larger urban areas where the population is concentrated. Such a program would tie in magnificently with forest management and would help in respect of thinning, planting and a return of our forests to the magnificence they possessed in their natural state.
I realize that the question which must be in the minister's mind in this regard, in view of the fact he is from the province of Quebec, concerns provincial jurisdiction. I suggest this kind of program would have to be a shared program, and that it could not be just one allowing a national group of individuals to run around in uniforms and work in the bush. I think the minister should approach this problem by working with one provincial forestry department which might be co-operative, such as the department of forestry of British Columbia or Ontario, and find out whether after a trial run of perhaps two years it would be possible to take a number of these people, who are looking for work and training under schedule 5, and are carried by the Department of Labour, in an attempt to develop a team of men who would receive training and perform useful work in our forests.
I can visualize a number of ways that this program could be tied in with ARDA. The minister will acknowledge that ARDA does allow a training program on a regional basis as far as financing is concerned. It seems to me that ARDA could be used in this way to provide the framework of a program to carry out this kind of thing.
Mr. Chairman, we need a minister of forestry who has sufficient imagination and drive to take advantage of this opportunity and move with it. I believe my suggestion is practical, although I realize one of the difficulties that was encountered in the United States in respect of the civilian conservation corps developed because it became a political football. Both the civilian conservation corps and the W.P.A. became political footballs. I remember the signs which hung in United States bars and which said: "Don't shoot it; it is not a bear, it is a W.P.A. worker having a sleep." That was the suggestion on the sign.

I agree that a program of this kind cannot be developed on a sound basis of the people who are to participate in it are a select group. Mr. Chairman, I can visualize the potentialities of such a program. Many good things could be done in this way and I recommend this idea to the minister as the second thing he should do as the Minister of Forestry.
The third thing I should like the minister to do is tackle the problems which face the forestry production industry in Canada. Surely the federal Department of Forestry, which is the senior department, should have some idea of the future need and demand for foresters in this country. There is considerable confusion in this regard. Recently in the lake-head area we have had discussions about attempts to establish a degree course in forestry. We have had a tremendous variety of prognostications in respect of the need for foresters, the required level of training for men who now know this industry in its entirety. We have also considered how far we must train individuals required in the different technical sections of this industry.
It seems to me that the forestry industry will continue to be the basic and most important element of our economy, and it is for that reason I suggest the minister could best become informed and enthusiastic about forestry in Canada by carrying out a study in respect of future needs in the field of forestry personnel. He should make this a very wide ranging project, because the situation is continually changing.
People have the conception that a forester is someone who wears a boy scout hat, high boots and travels around marking or blazing trees. It is a much more complicated field than that and it has much more variety. I think we need to know more about what our needs are in this field at the present time. Again, there is no central agency that really knows these things. Certainly the Canadian institute of forestry, which is the foresters' national organization, has really not come up with anything like this. I suggest to the minister it is with this organization he should co-operate and work in getting a draft of our future needs in terms of foresters and technicians. I think this would fit into the other two proposals I have put before the minister and I would hope they would at least interest him.
The one thing I would ask of the minister is that he would at least consider my suggestion seriously. I do not expect him to give the usual defence, what I might call the Henri Courtemanche defence, which would
Supply-Forestry
be to get up and read something prepared in rebuttal by his officials, pointing out all the worth-while little things that the Department of Forestry does or has done or plans to do. I have seen that in the department's annual report and in the publications that are listed here. I should like to suggest to the minister that we need something much bolder and more creative. He in particular more than anyone who is likely to fill that post has the opportunity, because for some reason he has the reputation. If the minister has been good enough to create the reputation, I think it is about time that, given the job he has, he began to come through and back it up with something solid.

Mr. Chairman, it is my intention to make a few brief observations in a general way with regard to the estimates of the department now before us. Others of my colleagues will be dealing with various aspects of the estimates and also with ARDA and the various programs to which reference has been made this afternoon. I should like to extend my congratulations to the minister on his appointment to this portfolio but in doing so I express some disappointment that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was transferred from the Department of Forestry to the Post Office Department. I believe he is a man of experience who was prepared to give definite and positive leadership in the department. I do not say that, however, with any intention of downgrading the present minister. I feel he will build upon the foundation laid by his predecessor, as his predecessor built upon the initial work of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in setting up the department.
As I have indicated, Mr. Chairman, I want to make some general remarks in regard to the Department of Forestry. I think we all recognize the fact that forestry is one of Canada's greatest industries. I suppose there are those in various parts of the country who will sometimes question that statement because of the fact that in their areas forestry does not particularly concern them. In fact, we were talking in a jocular fashion a little while ago and one of my colleagues said he did not have a tree in his constituency and therefore he would not presume to speak on forestry. Nevertheless I believe all of us in the house today recognize the tremendous importance of the forests and the forest industries to the Canadian economy.
Like one of the other speakers today I was somewhat disappointed that the minister did

Supply-Forestry
not take this opportunity to present a challenging program to us and outline some of the things he is contemplating as far as the development of the department is concerned. However, a very interesting pamphlet came to hand just recently from the Department of Forestry. It is publication No. 1002 titled "Canada, A Forest Nation". I think this is basically true. I should like to refer to several sections. It begins with the statement that Canada is a forest nation and the second paragraph reads as follows:
The total forested area of Canada is more than 1,700,000 square miles. Productive forests-those capable of producing usable timber-cover one million square miles. About 80 per cent of this forest land is publicly owned and administered by the ten provincial governments which make the forest crop available to the forest industries through a variety of systems. The remaining 20 per cent is made up of farm woodlots, forest land owned by companies and individuals, and of areas for which the federal government is responsible.
With respect to the annual forest harvest it states:
The annual harvest from the forest averages 3.200 million cubic feet.
Further on it states:
The forest industries employ over 300.000 and pay out $1,200 million in salaries and wages each year. Woods operations account for about $400 million in salaries and wages and provide employment in the neighbourhood of 80,000 man years, or the equivalent of 80,000 year round jobs.
Then it goes on to refer to the pulp and paper industry and to the fact that over a period of 50 years it has grown to become Canada's leading manufacturing industry. The pamphlet goes on to set out some of the important facts with relation to Canada as a forest nation. I think this information should be of real interest to many who come from sections of the country that are not forested. I give this information once again to indicate the fact that the minister has jurisdiction at least to a certain degree over one of Canada's greatest industries. I also wish to point out in this connection that even as forestry is one of Canada's great industries, so in my own province of British Columbia it occupies a very important place. The hon. member for Vancouver East interjects that British Columbia has 60 million acres of forest. I have here a pamphlet headed "British Columbia, Facts and Statistics, 1963". It contains some very interesting information with regard to British Columbia and I should like to put a few of these facts on the record. With regard to forestry it states:
The forests form the backbone of the British Columbia economy and contribute most to provincial income and employment. The estimated net

value of production of all forest industries amounted to $850 million in 1963, or approximately 38 per cent of total production.
The report goes on to state:
Of all manufacturing industries in British Columbia, lumber ranks first, pulp and paper ranks second, while plywood constitutes the fourth largest industry in the province. At present the British Columbia forest industries produce nearly 70 per cent of all the lumber manufactured in Canada-
I think this is something for us to appreciate.
-20 per cent of all the pulp, almost 15 per cent of all the paper, and approximately 85 per cent of all the plywood. The forest industries are an important source of employment. In 1963 they directly employed approximately 78.000 persons.
During the year 1962 British Columbia exported to foreign countries $602,400,000 worth of wood and wood products. Of this total, 75 per cent went to the United States, while 12 per cent went to the United Kingdom. The most important wood products exported in order of their value were: Lumber, $303,500,000: pulp, $123,600,000; newsprint. $105,900,000.
I think we in British Columbia have a tremendous heritage and a wonderful opportunity so far as this particular aspect of our economy is concerned. As I have pointed out, it is important not only to Canada but to British Columbia. Of course, as indicated by the percentage of the wealth that is accumulated from this source in British Columbia, there is a tremendous contribution in turn to our national economy.
Now. the entry of the federal government into the areas of activity and responsibility that have hitherto been considered of provincial concern now extends to forestry. I just read a booklet the other day pointing out the periods of time during which the federal government moved into certain areas that previously had been under provincial jurisdiction. It referred to national health and welfare, labour and the trend now to accept certain responsibilities with respect to the education of our people, especially in higher education. This trend has been extended now to forestry. Here, we come again to the importance of federal-provincial relations. Forestry comes under provincial jurisdiction, yet it seems as though the problems in this area are of such a magnitude, so widespread and so general across the country, that it seems advisable the federal authorities should assume some particular role so far as the development of our forests is concerned.
This was pointed out by the hon. member for Port Arthur as presenting one of the problems, the fact that we now have ten provincial jurisdictions and a federal jurisdiction. If there is going to be satisfactory progress made in the various fields of endeavour

there will have to be close co-operation and liaison maintained between federal and provincial jurisdictions. I do feel, however, as I have pointed out, that unquestionably the establishment of the federal Department of Forestry has been worth while. It has a legitimate function to perform so long as it is careful to confine itself to those matters outlined when the department was set up.
Reference has been made to the matter of conservation. We know that this is a very important part of forestry development in our country. If we do not have proper conservation and reforestation, then the time is going to come when we are not going to have any forests. This has been recognized by those who have been interested in this particular matter, and a great deal of attention has been given to it. I was reminded the other day, when there was a discussion taking place on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, that natural resources were included in the setting of the bases for the equalization grants, but no attention was given to the cost involved. The gross income was considered.
I should like to refer to a brief statement from a publication dealing with British Columbia forest industry facts, which states that the provincial government received $35 million in direct revenue, exclusive of income and sales taxes, from the sale of timber licences and stumpage in 1963, but the British Columbia forest services spent $17 million on all phases of its activities which included protection and the renewal of the resource. We see here therefore that in the province of British Columbia, and I imagine in other provinces that have extensive forest resources, a great deal of money is expended on the matter of conservation. I feel that in all of our discussions and in all of our negotiations we should remember, or the federal government should remember, that there is a great deal of money spent in conservation and promotion of these different things which should be taken into consideration. This includes, of course, fire protection to which the minister made reference in his introductory remarks.
There is just one other matter to which I should like to make a brief reference, and that is the matter of research. I think it is very necessary for research in this particular field to be accelerated. A certain amount is being done in universities by provincial governments. Then of course the industry itself is expending considerable amounts of money on research. However, the problems that affect the forest industry are more or less general. I suppose there are some local
Supply-Forestry
problems, but to a large extent the problems that affect the industry are country-wide, from one coast to the other. I feel there is a legitimate area here in which the federal department could expand its research facilities. The minister made some reference today to the fact that facilities are being extended in the province of British Columbia. We do appreciate this. As I pointed out, this is one of the fields in which I think those in the forest industry have a part to play. They could do so by pooling all their resources, pooling all their research facilities. Only in this way will adequate and effective progress be made in the field of research.
As I have stated, Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to make these brief remarks. Other matters will be dealt with when we come to the various items.

There is no department of the government of Canada that can better be described as the Cinderella department than the Department of Forestry. I do not believe I need to hold up the committee by reminding all Canadians that the forest industry, not only presently but for long years in the future, is the most important industry we have in Canada. Under the constitutional arrangement that we have, this industry is under the ownership, management and control of our ten provincial governments. The only direct control the federal government has in this field is in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
Having mentioned the simple realities of the background of the situation, I may say it has become increasingly clear in the last 15 years that something was drastically wrong with the handling of our forests in Canada. There is no need quarrelling about how this complicated situation developed. The fact remained that something had to be done. The reasons something had to be done were clear. In 1949, for example, the food and agriculture organization pointed out in its report that tremendously increased demands would be occurring in the world markets for products of the forests. This report in 1949 should have warned us in Canada that we, with our tremendous base of forest resources, should begin to plan for the day when we would be under pressure to supply the market.
In 1959 the food and agriculture organization of the world published its second report, pointing out once again in a revised form that the calculation on which the demand factor had been predicted in 1949 was wrong and it should have been much greater than had

Supply-Forestry
been indicated in 1949. It was on the basis of the 1959 report that the government of the day decided to do something about the challenge facing the forestry industry of Canada. We based our decision in setting up a new forestry department on the fact that demand by the people of the world for the products of the forests, primarily in paper products at that time but also in sawn lumber, would increase at such a rate that if something was not done in the lumber and paper producing countries of the world there would be a serious shortage all around the world. This was the first premise on which we worked.
The second premise on which we worked was that since the ownership of the forests and their management lay in the hands of the provincial governments, it was impossible for the officials of the branch of forestry, which was then in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, to deal on a basis of equality with ministers and deputy ministers at the provincial level. It seemed clear to us that if we were to take advantage of the opportunities that existed in the markets of the world for the products of the forests, we had to raise the status of this branch to the full level of having its own minister. It is, after all, our No. 1 industry; and this was done.
I would like to be able to say that in the intervening four years much progress has been made, but quite frankly I am appalled at how little has been done to meet the challenge of the opportunity that exists. As the hon. member for Port Arthur pointed out, you cannot move in the forest industry quickly and get the results you want. All your planning is based on 20, 30, 40 and even 100 years ahead, but the basic fact is that the demand is there, and just as the people of the world need food, so do they need the fibres of the forest.
In the Department of Forestry there is collected under one department three main branches. Each one of these branches, whether it be the forestry resource section, the pathology and entomology division or the forest products division, have concentrated in their respective divisions probably more brainpower and more dedication than any other department of government which we have. Yet with all this ability-undermanned, not supported fully by treasury board, not achieving what they should be able to achieve- in spite of all this tremendous asset, we are missing the boat.

To my mind the reason is very simple. Because they are restrained by the constitutional limitations on what they can do under the federal government, the tremendous achievements and accomplishments within this limited framework have not been sufficient to make a big impact on what I think is the crucial challenge before us.
The hon. member for Port Arthur pointed out what he thought was the problem. I can say this, and I think the minister will understand as his predecessor understood-this is not a partisan political criticism-that there is a problem and a challenge that has to be met, but it cannot be met by the minister's officials. This is a challenge to the minister. The responsibility rests on his shoulders, and if I may repeat a bit of what the hon. member for Port Arthur said, knowing from the minister's background and from the province of Quebec the difficulty he will have in the constitutional field, in spite of all the difficulties they place before him the country expects from the Minister of Forestry, to use the words of the hon. member for Port Arthur, such diplomacy, such charm, such practical inducements that he can lead these provincial departments, not only of forestry but all the ones that surround that industry, into the light of the opportunities that now exist. The opportunity is there. I said this to the minister's predecessor, that no minister in any government had a greater opportunity to serve his country well than did the Minister of Forestry.
What are some of the things that can be done to bring these provincial governments to see the light of opportunity? First of all they should be impressed with the fact that the federal government has a place in this picture, and the place the federal government has is in the marketing arena through the Department of Trade and Commerce. Second, it has a place in taxation policies, yes and even monetary policies, which have a direct bearing on the success or failure of getting the provincial governments, through their control of the forest licences, to do the things that the national interest demands.
A moment ago I mentioned the reports of F.A.O. in 1949 and 1959. So desperate is the situation that in 1964 F.A.O. did not choose to wait until 1969 for its regular decennial report, but issued a special report just a month ago, appealing to the whole world and warning the whole world not only of the impending shortage in pulp and paper products but also in sawn lumber.
Look at the figures of the proportions of use of wood products in Europe. Just a few

years ago 80 per cent of the forest production of Europe went into the sawn lumber section of the industry. Now that is rising to 90 per cent and 95 per cent, to meet the demand for sawn lumber as the people of Europe rehabilitate themselves and have better standards in their housing. Thus the demand for sawn lumber is rising at a very rapid percentage rate, and as they lessen the supply of wood production going into paper production this gives us an opportunity.
Just a few months ago I visited the mainland of China and in conversations I had with vice-ministers of that government one of the things they emphasized to me was that in addition to the farm machinery and fertilizer they needed for their 300 million acres of farmland, they had to face up to the practical fact that they would have to come into the markets of the world and buy newsprint in tremendous quantities. You can readily visualize why that is so.
Over there in the score of provinces in China the great forests of centuries ago were denuded and those which were left were burned off by the Japanese, with result that only two provinces have forestry reserves of any substance. You cannot take a nation of 700 million people and leave it without paper. What is the use of educating 80 million students in their schools unless there is something for them to read? How can they build up an industrial nation without the paper on which an industry is based? Here is one of the greatest demand factors that the world has faced in the last 10 years, and the only thing that stops unlimited purchases by the Chinese of paper and paper products in world markets is the fact that they have to earn the money to buy them; and they are desperately striving to do that. But here you have a demand factor. If the intentions of that government are going to be met, they want as a minimum to put a newspaper into every home in China. There are 700 million people in this one market, compared with 200 million in the United States and Canadian markets. Even if the newspaper that goes into those homes has only three or four pages, or even eight pages, as compared with our many-pages newspapers, the demand factor is tremendous.
When the Chinese look around the world for sources of supply they see the great forest reserves of Russia, but they know these forests will not meet their need because their products have not yet been adapted to the making of pulp and paper. They know that in the southeastern United States there is a
Supply-Forestry
potential for increasing production in pulp and paper because of the rapid growth of the forests in that part of the world due to the climate. But the potential is limited, in the face of this tremendous demand. They look at the heavy pressure on the forests of western Europe and see there is not much hope for them there. They look at the forests of the tropical areas of the world. They are not yet suitable for pulp and paper production on a large scale. Then they know that the one area in the world which can help them out is Canada, with its tremendous forest reserves.
How, then, I ask the minister, are you going to take opportunities like this, when as minister you have no control over the provincial governments except in regard to inducement in connection with markets? This is where the leadership test occurs. I think the minister should accept the fact that our paper industry, for instance, has grown up like Topsy and is to too large a degree integrated with the markets of the south. It is not a case of the production of a forest limit being available to buyers all over the world; the product of that timber limit is dedicated to the same newspaper in the United States every year. In too many cases this is so.
So far no provision has made any effort to change this situation. I am sure the minister also knows that, generally speaking, the forests of Ontario eastward are fairly well dedicated to some form of production right now. He knows that the only available virgin forest for pulp and paper production are in Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. These areas of the interior of British Columbia through to Manitoba cannot easily assimilate pulp and paper mills, even though there is a demand factor in the world for their production, because they are cut off from the place where the demand exists. The demand for pulp and paper products is first in Europe, where the growth rate is nearly 15 per cent per year. It is slowly and steadily increasing in the United States, I think by about 5 per cent. Then there are these virgin markets in China that I have outlined. But these areas cannot possibly get into those markets because they are in the centre of the continent. The mills on the eastern seaboard, on the St. Lawrence seaway and the coastal areas of British Columbia are to a large measure dedicated to southern market integration and their production is taken up by those markets.
I put these facts before the minister because on the basis of these facts, with the

Supply-Forestry
market opportunity here, with the system of marketing that is going on, X am sure the minister, with his reputation of getting over tremendous difficulties, can see the obvious solution to the problems. This one challenge met in the next five to ten years would be the greatest contribution that could be made by any minister of any department of any Canadian government, in dollars and cents; there is no question about it.
I do not know precisely how many more new mills we could develop in virgin forests. My guess would be, somewhere around 20, or maybe as high as 30; but that is all. Here we have a demand factor much greater than this extra number of mills could meet. This raises the proposal of the hon. member for Port Arthur. I know that the departmental officials all know that sooner or later this country has to turn its attention to systematic silviculture; but that is not going to come easily in view of this nice, comfortable rut into which the forest industry has got itself, particularly on the paper side, in dedicating its production to markets southward, when most of the new markets are eastward and westward.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the second challenge which the minister faces is how to make a breakthrough in this respect and induce the industry to look for greater marketing opportunities. The minister must impress upon the industry that in the long run not only will they be meeting the dividend requirements of their directors day by day or year by year, but there will be an increasing use of their products and a much greater production within the limits of their territory as the years go by-if not now, then 25 or 30 years from now.
The minister must use all the techniques at his command to get the industry to depart from the well established tradition of relying upon the type of cutting they carry out and leaving regeneration to nature. All this must be challenged. I am no scientist, Mr. Chairman, but I know enough about it to realize that the scientists can talk about it, write papers on it, and get no place. This is what is happening. The minister, with all the prestige of a federal ministry behind him, has to take the case to the industry, to the provincial ministers, and eventually to the people of Canada. He can do it if he will hold out the inducement of more money at the end of the rainbow. I do not think I was wrong when I said earlier in my remarks that the forest industry is the Cinder-

ella industry. Take it out of the kitchen and put it up at the top level.
I do not think there is any question about it; many of us would just love the opportunity of accepting this challenge and tackling the problem. I personally am envious of the minister, that he has this great opportunity in his grasp. If he does measure up to the opportunity, I will be the first to praise his name; but if he does not; I will be there as hard as I can go asking for action. He has one of the best groups of men ever collected around a minister. They will give him all the scientific information on production, control of disease, forest products research, and so on. But the minister's job is to realize that only he has the prestige, working within the limitations of the constituency, to get rid of these tremendous taboos that have been built up over the last 60 years and make a breakthrough in the ways I have suggested.
There are many sidelines I could lead the minister into. I do not think I would be wrong in suggesting that with all his opportunities, and in spite of the reluctance of the provinces-because they have treasury boards too-he could take much of the land in Canada which has no particular purpose and rededicate it to forest use. That might be done under the individual farm program, under ARDA, or through the county forests. But do not forget that it might also be done under the national forests. We have never moved into that field in Canada. There are arguments both for it and against it, but it cannot have escaped the minister's notice that in the last congress in the United States a bill went through one of the houses allowing the minister there to take over a ten year period some 50 million acres and add it to the national forests. The use of these national forests is not limited just to watching trees grow; it is also used for other purposes, mainly recreation.
In addition to that the hon. member for Port Arthur has spoken with some reason in expressing satisfaction regarding the tremendous contributions made by the civilian conservation corps in the United States in the 1930's. He suggested that we should take a look at this in Canada, and I agree with him. Not only do our forests lend themselves to a great business opportunity for the country, but they serve as a training course for young people not only from rural areas but from our cities, who have two months every year in which they could serve their country well. I do not follow things in the United

States closely but I understand that they expect to have one million people functioning under the youth conservation act the minute it goes through this year. Unfortunately, in Canada we could only speak of about 100,000; but these 100,000 could not only be used on work in the forests but could be tied in with the recreational and redevelopment activities around our cities and would provide a working force which would not only assist in their training but would also build assets for which there are markets at the end of the road.
I think I have said enough to indicate that there are some things which the minister will have in his mind, and I will be looking forward to the introduction of his bill in the house which will set up a new department. I do not blame him for reserving till that time his own personal philosophy, and for taking that opportunity to describe in some detail what he intends to do about these things. I hope that the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur and myself will have some bearing on the ideas which he will be presenting at that time.
While I am on my feet, although I may be a little out of order in asking for clarification, I should like to say now that I realize that much of this redevelopment work which will be done under ARDA will have to be through the forestry arm. Over the next few years we are going to require thousands of foresters, in the same way as over the years we have developed thousands of farmers. These foresters will be devoted to the shifting over from a very inefficient method, in my opinion, of handling forests into the more efficient methods of silviculture in areas close to civilization. In this field, which is purely within the hands of the provincial government, the key to the situation is that the federal minister can dangle before the provinces opportunities for markets. Where his persuasiveness will be really required is in the fact that the provinces will have a positive return.
If I may give an example, the province of Ontario puts 100,000 acres a year into reforestation. It is estimated that there are eight million acres as a minimum which should be shifted into forests in Ontario. At the rate they are going it will take 80 years. But the demand factor is on us now and in five or ten years the world will be in a precarious position in regard to supplying the needs of the woods section of the economy. I suggest that this matter is very urgent.
Supply-Forestry
If I may move a little further into this field, let me say I know the difficulties cannot be cured all across the country all at once. Under the ARDA concept you have an opportunity of selecting certain areas upon which you can concentrate. I have been watching the reports coming in from the interlake area and the news from Gaspe, and they have been getting the facts out. But on reading these reports I keep finding the prejudices of the past coming into them, even when people are supposed to have approached the subject completely from an all-resource use concept. In the report on the interlake area of Manitoba, which I assume the minister has seen, there is outlined the various opportunities for redeveloping the whole area between the two lakes in Manitoba. But they forgot the forestry part. If I were minister and paying half the cost of that study I would say: "Look, I don't mind paying half the cost, because this report came at the initiative of the province of Manitoba, but have you not forgotten something?" Forestry provides one of the great opportunities for redeveloping that area, and because the provincial authorities in Manitoba have been disappointed so often in the last 20 or 25 years about getting pulp and paper mills you cannot blame them in one sense for being disillusioned. However, it is the purpose of the minister to restore their faith and not to overlook the possibility of that type of use in the redevelopment of that area.
Likewise in the clay belts of Ontario and Quebec. I drove through that area last week end to look at it once again. In an area of good land where the farmers are farming good farms, I see 90 per cent of the area going back into natural forests. I know the land is good but they are suffering from a very simple missing ingredient-lack of markets. I know the initiative lies in the hands of the provinces under ARDA to make proposals, but that does not stop a livewire minister from having frequent chats with provincial ministers and telling them they are overlooking something. I should like to see a good land area on the northern slopes going to Hudson bay, James bay and Quebec. Take this area on as one where you realize that there is a market for these products which are there-beef and wood products. These may be combined. There are people there trained to do this sort of work. As the hon. member for Port Arthur mentioned, you have an Indian population which adapts itself to this type of work. Another area which I think is ideally suited,

Supply-Forestry
with good land but cursed with a lack of markets, is the Lake St. John area in Quebec. The whole area up from the Saguenay I should like to see looked at as an area like the Gaspe and the interlake area in Manitoba.
We accept the principle that the provinces must provide the initiative, but not the whole thing entirely. I suggest that the minister make a proposal to the provinces and they may bring forward something as a result. But it must be suggested. If two, three or four areas in Canada are being given the opportunity of going into pilot operations on a silviculture approach, this gives an opportunity to the trained men in the minister's department to work with the ARDA people and show that forestry can produce dollars and cents per acre in a superior fashion to what is now being produced from marginal agriculture and nutritional soil.
I thank you very much for allowing me the privilege of putting these ideas before the minister, because after the hon. member for Port Arthur had spoken I could not resist the opportunity of expanding his remarks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like the opportunity on the occasion of the minister's estimates being before the committee to take a few minutes of this committee's time to make a few remarks both to affirm some of the statements made just now by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and to discuss a particular problem related to forest and potential forest land in part of southern Ontario surrounding the city I represent.
Coming as I do from an entirely metropolitan riding perhaps I should establish my qualifications to make some remarks on this subject. I think possibly I may claim a more intimate and longer standing association with the federal government forestry branch than almost any member of the house, being the son of a man who was an employee of the federal forestry branch for 40 years, ultimately becoming a director. I have heard from him and his associates many expressions of the frustrations about which we have just heard from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in respect of the problem created by division of jurisdiction over Canada's forest resources, and the particular frustrations of people with scientific training in forestry and related sciences who see what Canadian forests are capable of, what they require and the way in which they are failing to receive the attention they deserve.

One particular area that seems of importance to me, and that I should like to stress today, relates to some of the marginal lands, some of the worked out lands, and some of the farm lands in southern Ontario stretching right from the Quebec border to lake Huron which, initially cleared as long ago as a century, or a century and a half, have over a period of time been worked out or by maltreatment ceased to be productive for farm purposes.
I think it has been clearly established over a period of years, including consideration by the Senate committee on land uses in Canada, that there is a great potential for this land, and a great opportunity for various levels of government to introduce and encourage reforestation of these lands, which perhaps should never have been taken out from under forest cover in the first place. A great many recommendations in respect of the development of these lands have called for intervention of governments. I point out there is a great deal of initiative on the part of private operators, and chiefly individuals who have over a period of years both for profit and purely on the basis of a hobby, established tree farms in areas where they have engaged in reforestation in an attempt to put these lands again under tree cover.
One of the difficulties that has stood in the way of people carrying on this enterprise has been the manner in which, over a period of years, property assets represented by these reforestation projects, have been treated for tax purposes. In this respect the federal government does not have sole and absolute jurisdiction.
The first difficulty arose in that area which might generally be described as death duties where both the federal government, by way of estate tax, and the provincial government, by way of succession duties, have levied taxes against the assets of deceased persons. The remarks I have made I address both to the Minister of Forestry and his colleague the Minister of Finance, for consideration at the time of the budget. I would also suggest that the Minister of Forestry keep these ideas in mind for consideration when he is next talking with provincial governments in respect of agreements between federal and provincial governments which are initiated on the basis of the present statute, and which were originally negotiated on the basis of the Canada Forestry Act.
The chief effect, I would suggest, of the present arrangement in respect of estate

taxes and succession duties is the encouragement of bad forestry practices because of the necessity of recovering cash to pay these estate taxes and succession duties. The necessity for a quick turnover so that the claims of the crown can be satisfied means that bad forestry practices may often be followed and land that has, with great care, been brought slowly along to the point where it might be put to a sustained yield basis, may for example have to be subject to strip cutting altogether, or other bad forestry practices which will yield an immediate or early cash return. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it deserves the consideration of both the federal and provincial tax authorities, to see how, by constitutional arrangements and related legislation, changes can be effected, making it possible to postpone the payment of succession duties and estate taxes until such time as, in accordance with good forestry practice, the forest crop on any particular land is realized. In the case of lands which are on a sustained yield basis I suggest a formula could be worked out for periodic payment of succession duties and estate taxes or, if it is land on which the forest is ultimately brought to maturity and is going to be cut clear, then at such time the estate taxes or succession duties which may have been outstanding, with added interest, could become payable.
At the same time, I would suggest that municipal taxes may have a serious effect on tree farming and tree farmers in our different provinces, and that efforts should be made to recast the structure of municipal taxes so they recognize the special character of a forest. As hon. members know, land devoted to forestry may for very many years, in accordance with good forestry practice, not yield any income at all. But, as we all know, nothing is more certain than that each year the county tax assessor will be around to collect his mite from the owner of the land.
Mr. Chairman, what I am suggesting again today is that the payment, or if not the payment perhaps the assessment arrangements under provincial legislation, could be changed so that the assessment and payment of municipal taxes could be postponed until the crops from the particular land is realized, in accordance with good forestry practice.
In respect of these various amendments, and for inspiration in connection with this type of amendment, I would suggest the minister and his department could possibly look to some of the measures which have 20220-451i
Annual Vacations Act
been enacted in the United Kingdom in recent years for the purpose of encouraging the owners of particular lands to maintain them under forest, and to follow good forestry practices. In particular I would refer the minister to the provision in the United Kingdom death duty legislation which defines timber and agricultural land, or that devoted to timber in a particular way, at the lower rate which is applicable to that part of a person's estate which is under forest. I think both the provincial and federal governments should seriously consider this kind of amendment to our taxation statutes, which in the long run I suggest would ultimately lead to the same revenue but would adjust the structure of the taxation in such a way as to be consistent with the manner in which these very valuable resources by Canadians should be developed and realized.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is five o'clock. I will therefore wait until the next opportunity to make my remarks.

Progress reported.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
