speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-54, to amend the Annual Vacations Act (three weeks after five years).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple and straightforward bill, the entire purport of which is contained in the title. The bill proposes to amend the Annual Vacations Act which is already on the statute books, to provide that an employee with five years employment shall have three weeks annual vacation with pay. As hon. members are aware, at the present time the act provides for one week after one year and for two weeks after two years of employment. The present act goes no further. But in this day and age a great many people, especially those who have served for any period of time, do have a longer vacation each year than two weeks, and it seems to many of us that such

Annual Vacations Act
a provision ought to be part of our national labour legislation.
I hope it can be clear at this time, because it has not always been clear with respect to these bills of mine, that this does not refer to civil servants. It does not refer to federal employees. It refers to workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction. I mention that because on two or three occasions when I have had companion bills before the house I have read the next day in the press that the member for Winnipeg North Centre was again trying to get something more for federal civil servants. I do that in its place, Mr. Speaker; but this is general labour legislation which applies to all those workers in Canada the nature of whose employment is such that they come under federal labour jurisdiction. These include railway, transportation and communications workers, bank employees and quite a long list of others. The list has been put on the record a number of times.
Although the list is a long one we know that labour matters in this country are the subject of divided jurisdiction. Some come under federal jurisdiction, some come under provincial jurisdiction. Roughly speaking, about one tenth of the labour force comes under federal labour jurisdiction and the remaining 90 per cent come under provincial jurisdiction.
The purpose of this bill is to improve a piece of federal legislation that we already have. Actually, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the request, if I may call it that, made in this bill is a very reasonable one. In fact, it is so reasonable I am almost ashamed of it. Instead of asking for three weeks vacation with pay after five years I think the bill should have asked for three weeks after three years or four years at the most. But around this place one has to learn to expect things to move slowly, especially with the 1919 Liberals still in power, and so if we could get this much at least it would be a bit of progress.
But I say, Mr. Speaker, that no one can deny the utter reasonableness of this proposal. It is not breaking new ground as to principle. The principle is already established that by federal labour legislation we declare that workers who come under that jurisdiction should have holidays with pay. So far we have provided just two definitions. We say that those who have worked for one year shall get one week's vacation with pay and we say that those who have worked for two years shall get two weeks vacation with pay. It is our contention that we should widen this definition and say that those who have worked

for five years shall get at least three weeks vacation with pay.
Because this proposition is so reasonable I hope that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), who I see in his place and who as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour will no doubt be replying, will treat it in the simple, straightforward, reasonable manner in which it is presented. I hope he will not give us another of those profound orations that go all around the subject but fail to deal with the simplicity and straightforwardness of the proposal. I do not know whether he can do it but I throw out the challenge to him. He has been on his feet a lot this week and has had a good deal of practice. I suggest that today he come up with something new, and what he really ought to come up with is an admission that this proposition is so reasonable that the government is prepared to accept it. If he cannot do that, the least it can do is to ask the house to refer the subject matter to the committee for that further study that is so often a way out for the government.
One of the other answers that the parliamentary secretary no doubt will make is that this is an item in a national labour code and why does the member for Winnipeg North Centre not wait for the national labour code and see if this provision is not included in that code? As the hon. member for Kootenay East knows, I have been waiting and waiting and waiting. For a while he sat over on this side of the house and he complained about having to wait and wait and wait. At the moment I am not going to rehearse the long wait it has been for most of my lifetime, since 1919, but I remind the parliamentary secretary and the house of how difficult it is to get action on this simple matter at this session of parliament.
As everyone knows, in the last session of parliament, the first after the 1963 election, we were told categorically we would get a labour code at this session of parliament. Sure enough, when we met on February 18 it was promised in the speech from the throne. That promise is to be found on page 2 of Hansard for February 18. Two days later the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and as found on page 57 of Hansard he underlined during the course of his speech this promise in the speech from the throne, a national labour code, and said it would be brought forward at this session.
Four days later the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) spoke in the same debate and as

recorded on page 157 he confirmed that a national labour code would be brought in at this session. In the meantime we have had many weeks, many months, of the session, and where are we getting? On April 21 I asked the Minister of Labour for about the umpteenth time if we could expect the national labour code to be put on the order paper soon. His reply was that it would appear on the order paper "as quickly as possible". That is to be found on page 2397 of Hansard for April 21. We let a few weeks go by, but because "as quickly as possible" did not seem to be very fast I asked a similar question on July 13 and the answer is to be found on page 5380 of Hansard where the Minister of Labour said that the national labour code would be on the order paper "soon".
On August 4, as recorded at page 6351 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) if we were not going to get this on the order paper soon in view of his promise that it was coming soon. Some members will recall that he replied that I was misquoting him; that it had not been promised soon, but only as soon as possible. Well, there is a fine distinction between those phrases. When I was able to show the minister that he had said "soon" on one occasion, he came back with that interesting quip to be found on page 6351 of Hansard, that it would be on the order paper as soon as possible, and he hoped that would be soon.
Well, as the parliamentary secretary knows, I asked the minister a question about this matter this afternoon on orders of the day. He was still unable to give an answer as to when this matter would be on the order paper. I must say that in reply to one question I got a definite, one word answer, "Yes". What was the question to which that reply was made? The question was, will it be on the order paper at this session? I see my genial friend, the parliamentary secretary, nodding his head confirming what the Minister of Labour said. How long is this session going to last? It could be the longest session in history. Sessions have been known to last over three calendar years. There is no requirement that a session be prorogued so long as there are items on the order paper with which the government wants to proceed. This session may go on interminably.

speechtext:
In so far as the subject matter is concerned, we have already pointed out to the house that there should be a considerable amount of research given to this matter of the type that has been undertaken by the Department of Labour. This research should be directed toward the length of the vacation, and after how many years of service it should be given. The hon. gentleman did not go into that question at all, although in his research he may have done so. At any rate, I believe he would agree that there should be research conducted into these questions. How much vacation should a worker receive and after how long a period of work?
The principle has been rather widely accepted in collective bargaining for some years that there should be a gradual extension of vacation periods according to the length of service of the employee. I suggest this is a recognized principle, that the worker who stays a long time on one job has some sort of vested interest. He perhaps builds a home in the area and so perhaps becomes more settled in that particular region. He puts his children into the schools of that region to which they become accustomed. In general, he is contributing more, acquiring more of a vested interest in that particular position. By the same token, he may or may not be progressing on the salary scale by staying on the job over the years. I feel this is a sound

principle and he is entitled to a greater amount of vacation.
The hon. gentleman's formula suggests that after five years service three weeks should be granted. Certainly, as many members of the house know, there are collective agreements in the country today that do provide three weeks vacation after five years. There are collective agreements that provide four weeks after ten years and some provide four weeks after 20 years. This is an extension of the principle. There is a great deal of variety in the provisions of collective agreements in this country today concerning the length of the vacation period. Certainly I feel, despite the fact that the hon. member has pointed out only one out of ten Canadian workers is subject to federal jurisdiction, that it is desirable to extend this principle. A great many of these people are covered by pretty good collective agreements and I refer, for example, to the railway employees. Other employees should have something comparable.
Even so, I think it is good that the federal parliament should be concerned about this question. The federal parliament, in general, should show the way for the provinces when it comes to minimum standards for employee benefits of this type. I think that this is the next best thing we can do to having full jurisdiction. As the hon. member pointed out, there is divided jurisdiction today and, as a consequence, our legislation directly affects only very few.
I would be accused by some of my hon. friends of being a centralist if I said it is a shame that all the workers in the country are not subject to federal legislation with regard to labour standards, but I think it is unfortunate that there is not uniformity in this regard across the country. I think federal legislation as it has existed in the past, and as it will be in the labour code which will be presented for discussion this session, is a good thing to show the way to provinces, and I would hope those provinces that do not have as good legislation would see fit to fall in line as time passes.
Dealing with the progressive philosophy of such legislation I would point out that there are many people in Canada who are not subject to the protection of trade unions, and many who do not have the benefits of collective bargaining agreements, people who are at the mercy of their employers. But let me hasten to say that sometimes the employer is a very benevolent man or company and takes good care of them. Unfortunately that is not so in other cases. In England, on the

other hand, a higher percentage of the working population has always been subject to collective agreement. Over the years in that industrialized economy there has been such a history and tradition of trade unionism that even those who are not protected by a trade union, because the number involved may be too small for a union to be effective, are by custom and tradition covered by the principles of the legislation.
Unfortunately we in Canada find that something less than 25 per cent, or some such small percentage of our workers are unionized, and there are whole areas of the country where many people are employed in small industries, in the retail trades and other work, who do not have the protection of collective bargaining. This type of legislation, and that which will be included in the national labour code to be presented by the Minister of Labour, will be important to these people because it will provide them with that sort of protection. It gives them coverage by law that other employees sometimes receive by negotiation through collective agreements.

subtopic: ADDRESSES AT OPENING OF THIRD COMMONWEALTH EDUCATION CONFERENCE

speechtext:
Address of the Prime Minister, The Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson when welcoming the delegates to the third commonwealth education conference, House of Commons, Ottawa, Friday, August 21, 1964.
It is my pleasant duty today to welcome you, as I do most warmly, on behalf of the Canadian people and government, to the third commonwealth education conference.
As you open your 15-day conference, I do not envy you your assignment. I confess that there have been occasions in the last 30 years or so when I have felt that the teaching profession had many advantages over diplomacy or politics; and that I hadn't sufficiently appreciated my good fortune many years ago, when I was on the faculty of the University of Toronto. But when I look at the challenge facing today's educators; when I look at the problems confronting you, I am forced to conclude that my escape from a teaching career may not have been such a misfortune for me after all.
The objectives and the agenda of your conference are certainly impressive. For man's every goal-the good life, happiness, security, even global peace-depends in the end on education; on closing the "education gap" which is fundamental to every other gap.
It is encouraging to see in such a conference as this, delegates from all continents and races, working together in harmony and partnership in a cause so vital to mankind's future, We welcome, along with the representatives of 17 independent members of the commonwealth, delegates from many British dependencies and territories-some 16, I believe. The progress of these regions toward independence and, if they so desire, commonwealth membership-and the development of their resources to sustain the obligations of independence- is a source of deep satisfaction to us all.
This march of colonies to independence is also a fine tribute to Great Britain's enlightened record of "disengagement from empire"; one that others in the world might emulate.
Before your conference president delivers the inaugural address, perhaps I may be permitted to add to these remarks of welcome a few observations on the recent commonwealth prime ministers' conference which was attended by leaders of governments representing
people of diverse races, cultures, creeds and colour, from all parts of the world. The conference made several proposals which will, I am sure, be before you for consideration.
-proposals for new, co-operative development projects; for additional study of techniques in administration and development planning.
-proposals for the possible formation of a new institute to provide specialized training and research to senior administrators concerned with development problems in new countries;
-proposals for strengthening existing commonwealth programs; for promotion-possibly through a commonwealth foundation-of interchanges and closer contacts within professions;
-proposals for a commonwealth medical conference;
-proposals for possible forms of technical assistance to the developing countries which would permit them to participate in the establishment and use of a global system of satellite communications.
Even more significant evidence of the spirit that guides the nations of the new commonwealth in their co-operative endeavours, was the prime ministers' agreement on the importance of the commonwealth's attitude to those interracial problems which threaten the orderly development of mankind.
"As a community of many different races", the prime ministers said, "the commonwealth is itself an almost unique experiment in international co-operation among people of several races and continents."
The co-operation we seek depends primarily on mutual understanding; and understanding is the goal of all education. We made progress toward that goal in London, in the "declaration on racial equality" which was unanimously and wholeheartedly accepted.
The importance of and the need for such a declaration of racial co-operation and equality was never more apparent. Racial discrimination and the intensification in many areas of mutual fear between races must be, for us all, one of the most disturbing features of the present world situation; the root cause of difficulty and danger in many unsolved problems.
The problem of course exists both within and outside the commonwealth. But obviously

if the commonwealth could not meet its own challenge, confidence in our brave experiment would have been badly shaken, if not destroyed-not only among our own members, but among other millions of people who see in the commonwealth example their best hope for co-operation between races.
With this in mind-and I am quoting from the communique-"The prime ministers affirmed their belief that, for all commonwealth governments, it should be an objective of policy to build in each country a structure of society which offers equal opportunity and non-discrimination for all its people, irrespective of race, colour or creed. The commonwealth should be able to exercise constructive leadership in the application of democratic principles in a manner which will enable the people of each country of different racial and cultural groups to exist and develop as equal citizens."
Canada of course takes a special pride in this conference; in the progress made in this field during the past five years. The decision for a commonwealth conference on education came on the initiative of the Canadian government of the day in 1958. This fact naturally makes us feel doubly privileged to have this third conference here, in our capital.
In the progress made in carrying out the four co-operative programs recommended by the first conference at Oxford, this country has demonstrated its faith in and willingness to help underdeveloped and emerging countries and people. I can assure you that we will continue to do that.
As part of this objective, we wish to help make other nations educationally self sufficient. So an ever increasing proportion of our increasing aid programs goes directly for educational purposes.
In the next two weeks you will be assessing the results of this co-operation recommended by previous conferences. You will be recommending ways to improve present forms of assistance; weighing new proposals against problems seemingly defiant of any solution. You will again be asking whether in a world in which no country has enough scholars and teachers, the limited supply of those who can help should be reduced by sending them to the developing countries to teach and to assist, in the establishment of basic programs of study; or whether it would not be better to bring more of the students and scholars from the developing countries to train in established facilities outside their new borders. Both are necessary. But an expert judgment of what the proportions should be, one to the other, would be helpful.
You have before you an agenda which would make the wisest and most energetic blanch. I congratulate the liaison council and the liaison unit on putting forward such a challenging agenda and on their planning and organization of the conference. Among the subjects for committee discussions, I notice that for the first time, the uses of mass media-television, films, tape recordings; the uses of electronic sound and sight-in education-are to be considered. The potential here, of course, staggers the imagination. It will in time affect almost everything you are discussing. It can be the most significant method ever devised for closing the educational gap at a rate beyond our fondest hopes. But it can also become the most frightening of all the results of modern technology in its tendencies to "dehumanize" society.
Before concluding, may I say how fortunate we have been to secure as president of the conference one of our outstanding and most distinguished citizens, Right Hon. Vincent Massey. My own deep respect and admiration for him is shared by all Canadians and indeed by all who know him. His long and brilliant career of public service as educator, in the broadest sense, businessman and diplomat was climaxed when he became, as Governor General, the first Canadian representative of the monarch in Canada.
I am honoured and privileged to welcome you to Ottawa and I am delighted now to be able to turn the conference over to its president.
Address given by Right Hon. Vincent Massey, C.H., at the opening of the third commonwealth education conference, Ottawa, Friday, 21st August, 1964.
My first words must be of gratitude for the honour of being asked to preside at the third commonwealth education conference. As a Canadian, I welcome you to this country, which is proud to be your host for the meeting; as president of the conference, which is so important for all our countries, I welcome you to this opening session.
Allow me to use our other official language to wish a most sincere and cordial welcome to French speaking members of the conference.

Many of you will not have been in this country before. I am glad to know that a number of you will be travelling in Canada

when the conference is over. So that you will better understand what you see, I should like to tell you a little about the background. Here, as elsewhere in the world today, the one certain thing is change. In the course of my own lifetime, I have seen Canada evolve from an agricultural economy to a largely industrial one; from a colony to a sovereign state; from a country with no foreign relations to one represented in over 60 nations.
We have a complicated national pattern. We are a land of many cultures. There is a large French part, a large English part and a host of smaller ethnic parts. Every part by itself is a minority, separate and distinct. Quebec is the home of French culture in North America and so is more than just one of our ten provinces. Some say that our plural society is a mosaic; others call it a salad. Canada in recent years has received great waves of immigration from Europe, increasing our population since the second world war by more than two millions, but these newcomers have not been caught up and reshaped-differences are welcomed here. In spite of this increase, you may be struck by the fact that our population is small for so large a country-even that which we have is, to some extent, reduced by emigration. Many immigrants have made Canada a stopping point on their way to the United States, and many native born Canadians have moved south. Though immigration surpasses emigration, it does not fully replace the skills and drive of those we lose.
Canadian life has been influenced to an extent we sometimes hardly realize by the fact that we are a northern country. This is reflected in the way we live and, indeed, in our national character. We lie between two giant neighbours and are flanked by two great oceans opening out to the occidental and oriental worlds; this results in as many problems as advantages. In Canada there are six time zones across our 4,500 miles of breadth, and we require systems of transportation and communications which would be regarded as unjustified were it not for the fact that national unity demands the east-west links which offset the ever-present pull to the south.
Canada is a monarchy, indeed, she has been since her beginning, whether the crown was French or English. Now the crown of the kingdom of Canada is Canadian. We are really not a young or shapeless country. We are in our fourth century of settlement and are about to celebrate the hundredth anniversary of our constitution. That document is today one of the oldest constitutions in the world continuously in force. It establishes the principle
of "peace, order and good government". This time-honoured objective was chosen in preference to the alternative formula "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness'". The choice indicates a society founded upon allegiance instead of social contract, a society reflecting the organic growth of tradition itself rather than one created by an explicit act of reason or will.
Canada has practically no revolutionary background, few national myths and folk heroes. Her existence has always been too precarious, her dependence upon "mother countries" always too real, and her peoples' jealousy of their cultural heritages too intense to permit flirtations with adventure. However, as you will be aware during your sojourn here, we are now passing through one of those periods which most countries, and all federations, experience, of constitutional and political strain and readjustment to a new equilibrium. The hereditary sense of tolerance and compromise which has enabled us to carry on over the generations will, I have no doubt, ultimately help us to settle the questions which today beset us. We have learned tolerance in a hard and practical school. As a Canadian writer has said, "Not only was this country formed out of ... defeated racial and political groups; some of these groups had once been bitter enemies of one another.. .and they had to live in peace ..."
However, compromise in Canadian life has always somewhat blurred our image of ourselves, and has often discouraged bold initiatives in nation building. Through the early years another handicap was our status as a dependency. But this has not been without its compensations. Having been a colony ourselves, we understand more acutely the feelings of those who travel a road with which we are already familiar. Our only wars have been in self defence or for the liberation of other peoples. Our tradition has been peaceable, without even internal strife except enough to remember and fear its possibility.
The result of history, geography and colonization is that there are attitudes and things which are peculiarly Canadian, Canada did not just happen. It was built and is maintained by the concerted efforts of her people. Western and northern Canada have been a workshop, planned and ordered by government and business established in advance of settlement.
For national schemes we have employed the device of the crown corporation, a semiindependent governmental body containing features of both public and private enterprise.

Yet the result-though socialistic-has not been socialism, perhaps because here the public is suspicious of "state planning" and "nationalization". The technique of the crown corporation, a characteristic Canadian compromise, may well be of value to countries with similar problems.
Another result of the Canadian experience that may interest other developing nations is our practice of federalism. Although our loose federal constitutional structure, with vast areas of power vested in the provincial governments, has sometimes made it difficult to tackle some national problems, it has allowed the establishment and development of a single state in which the two major European cultures and a host of minorities have co-existed and flourished.
This confederation is one of the two great political experiments with which Canadians have been concerned. The other one to which we have made a significant contribution is the commonwealth itself, for its pattern of independence, growing from responsible government, was first developed here in Canada a century ago. The peculiar constitutional principles which caught on in the whole empire, and transformed it, emerged as we solved our own relations with the mother country; we became a constitutional laboratory in which the nineteenth century empire was created. The new commonwealth after the second world war was built on ideas of association which Canadians advocated in opposition to those of imperial federation and a united front which found favour in some quarters in Great Britain and the other dominions.
The plural and diverse communities of other commonwealth countries have much in common with this one. In unfeignedly welcoming the new countries to their independence, congratulating them on their achievement and wishing them every happiness and success for their people, we Canadians also hope to be known as understanding and helpful. Like Canada, the more recent members have been formed by practical compromise through a process of evolution, rather than by the application of logic. Indeed, this process is still being adapted to the commonwealth's growing number of member countries. Though necessary and unavoidable, the growing pains of nationhood are always difficult and sometimes severe. They are not unknown to us. One of the great indefinable bonds of the commonwealth is the special and active interest assured to new members in facing the difficult problems that are
bound to arise in setting up a sovereign country.
I am one of those who believe in the commonwealth-I admire its concept and respect its functions; as a Canadian I am proud of it-any of us who have been concerned with its growth could hardly feel otherwise. The commonwealth began here when three colonies in British North America were federally united in 1867. A few years before Sir John Macdonald, the principal architect of what became Canada, said:
"We are fast ceasing to be a dependency, and are assuming the position of an ally of Great Britain. England will be the centre, surrounded and sustained by an alliance not only of Canada, but Australia, and all her other possessions; and there will be thus formed an immense confederation of freemen, the greatest confederacy of civilized and intelligent men that has ever had an existence on the face of the globe."
From these origins we have passed through four identifiable stages. First, from the British North America Act of 1867 to the statute of Westminster of 1931-the so-called "old commonwealth", about which Sir Wilfrid Laurier observed in 1907, "The proper basis of the British empire was that it was to be composed of a galaxy of nations under the British crown."
Second, from the statute of Westminster to the independence of India and Pakistan, involving the beginnings of the "new" commonwealth with its republican members. Mr. Nehru, so sorely missed by all of us, said in 1950:
"We are members of the commonwealth- that rather strange and odd collection of nations which seems to prosper most in adversity-it does teach us many lessons, and in the sense that we get on best together when we meet in complete freedom and comradeship and we know that there is going to be no pressure or compulsion exercised upon us."
Third, from the independence of India to the establishment of Malaysia, the widening of the "new" commonwealth.
Fourth, there remains a period of adjustment in many places. In this last stage, the great decolonizing function of the commonwealth is being concluded. Its shape and boundaries have now been more or less defined. There only remains a time of mutation or consolidation.
Realizing what we have to work with, we must decide what we wish to do with it. Now is the moment of our greatest opportunity. To know what we should do, it is

worth considering what we are and where we are going.
In the last 17 years the commonwealth has grown from five independent countries to nearly 20. The 70 million people in this group of nations have increased to 700 million-a quarter of the world's population.
Many attempts have been made to define this association of countries. Mr. John Holmes, the head of our institute of international affairs, has spoken of it as:
"an association among countries of various races and continents which, in spite of wide differences of political practice and international orientation, share, as a result of a common historical experience, certain constitutional and legal attitudes, governmental and business practices and habits of working together. It is a matter of faith and will."
Many adjectives have been applied to the commonwealth. It has been called "shapeless, unorganized, unstructured, anomalous, illogical". Some of our more advanced theologians have even suggested that we accept the inevitable, dismantle the traditional apparatus, abolish the nomenclature, and suppress the ritual in the hope that the essential faith will survive in hibernation to re-emerge in its own time, transformed and revitalized. Others say that there is no chance of survival at all, that the commonwealth is fit for nothing but the reminiscences of aging statesmen. An anonymous writer, not very long ago, delivered himself of an utterance, rather less than statesman-like, when he said "The commonwealth has really become a gigantic farce."
Of course it is not only in Great Britain that some politicians would seek to blame the commonwealth connection for one or other or indeed all of their domestic ills. There will always be those who dream of solving their problems by denying their duties and historical or sentimental attachments, to seek the illusory freedom of total irresponsibility, predicated upon no principle higher than a policy of pure self interest. That is not our way. Because there is implicit in the concept of the commonwealth, values of duty and honour and service, no definition of it can be wholly satisfactory. It is much easier to say what it is not than to say what it is. It has been described as a club, but a club has certain set rules and obligations which the commonwealth does not possess, at least so far. It is not a power bloc. It is not a diplomatic unit. It is not an economic force. It is not even a group of like minded people or of like minded nations, and yet in a sense
it can sometimes be those things, although it is none of them. It does confer certain economic advantages on its members. In fact, the commonwealth is often justified in some countries by the expectation of more favourable economic terms. It has also political advantages. Canada uses it as a counterbalance to the United States. Perhaps for this reason, Canadians may have been guilty of underestimating the economic factor and stressing the political. Certainly the commercial and financial advantages of membership have, for many years, been of rather less importance to Canada than to other members. The commonwealth has also certain military advantages. A number of recent incidents have shown the readiness of members to help one another, even in the absence of formal treaty commitments.
Besides these non-sentimental realities, we are also a network of personal relationships. A recently published handbook named 85 organizations and societies in Britain alone concerned with various aspects of commonwealth relations and the list is certainly far from exhaustive. These organizations, ranging from the commonwealth collection of microorganisms, to the consultative space research committee, reach their apex at the prime ministerial level. Regular meetings and constant interchanges of information are as valuable as their results are immeasurable. After all, we have in this room today a vivid example of how the commonwealth can be put to work.
Such relationships and advantages are not in themselves the commonwealth. They are components but they give us only glimpses of the whole. It remains an almost completely informal association and this, in many ways, is perhaps its greatest merit. Lacking rigidity, it cannot be shattered by a blow in any one place. The commander in chief of Hitler's navy reported in September, 1940, "The British empire is not expected to collapse owing to the peculiar innate force of the political objectives embodied in the commonwealth of nations".
Through its development since the war, the commonwealth has shown striking adaptability. Indeed, to quote a recent comment, " ... one of the most persistent of illusions is that it is essentially a conservative and stable institution. In fact, it is a supreme triumph in wild, zestful, fantastic innovation." Making a virtue of necessity in accordance with its genius, the commonwealth today glorifies its diversity and freedom from commitment. It possesses what has been called

"invertebrate informality". It finds its virtue not in unity of policy but in a search for understanding, for the sharing of views and constant consultation among its members.
It is often asked what is the value of these functions; has the commonwealth any future? It is important to remember that it does exist, and that it influences the international relationships of each of its members. Those who have experienced it believe in it, and their attitude must be recognized as partially a matter of faith. The fact that the mystique is difficult to define and unacceptable to some critics, does not mean that it can be discarded.
The United Kingdom's negotiations with the common market tore the last shred of illusion away from the commonwealth. It was a moment of truth when the full extent of the post-war revolution had to be recognized and accepted. Many are now realizing that what then seemed a death rattle was, in fact, a birth pang of a new stage in our development.
The shape of the commonwealth and the full contrast of its diverse interests, have been borne in upon us. Aware of our differences, and of the realities of our situation, we can see that we none the less form the only grouping of nations which bridges the many divisions of a much divided world. The rich and the poor, the east and the west, the tropical and temperate, the developing and the developed-all these are contained in our family grouping. We have on hand a supreme opportunity to help one another and to set an example for other countries in the mending of these differences that threaten our existence.
For the commonwealth to meet the challenge of mutual assistance, it must be recognized that each country has a responsibility in leadership. Although to do this we must abandon the idea of the commonwealth as an English institution, no one will ever forget the greatness of the British legacies. The railways, harbours and industries which Britain built are far less important than the institutions of government, above all the values which she brought to our peoples, and left with them. These have made the deepest impact. Today the greatest testimony to British genius can be seen in the civil service, the judiciary, the armed forces and even the playing fields, which stand for the finest in British traditions. It is a record that history is unlikely to ignore. It will be remembered with the contributions of Greece and Rome to world civilization. But the past must not be allowed to dominate the present. As Professor Silcock of the University of Malaya said not long ago;
"The commonwealth is no longer a wheel with only one centre of force and drive. If it is to survive at all, it will be as a lattice of increasing intercommunications and interaction. No monopoly of initiative and concern should be expected of the government, the people or the press of the 'mother country'."
To draw people together is, of course, the function of the United Nations and it has sometimes been said that its existence makes the commonwealth unnecessary. The answer is that the ties which hold the races and continents in contract are frail and tenuous enough; every reinforcement is worth while and among other contemporary international organizations with which it can and should be compared, the commonwealth has shown more internal consistency than any other. As Mr. Nehru pointed out at the time, India did not leave the commonwealth over the Suez incident because, in his view, it would have been a retrograde step to sever any link that exists between nations.
Though there may be impatience and trespasses upon civil liberties among member states, one can ask how much worse things might be without the commonwealth influence. In all our countries there is a substantial body of opinion-conscious of the sins we have committed in the name of effective government, of the mixed history of colonial rule, of racial intolerance-which insists that we must not expect all the traditions of Westminster in countries where unity is frail, illiteracy is high, and the economy a baffling puzzle. There should be patience and good intention in watching and helping others to solve the paradoxes that beset the final stages of colonialism in various comers of the world. If our multiracial fraternal society has any reason for existence, the most immediate is to resolve these problems.
Our way is to take a pragmatic route to the realization of higher ideals. We cannot all have the same constitutional mechanisms. But, equally, we must not expect too much of the commonwealth's now respectably established tradition of limitless elasticity. Though all nations must work out their own salvation, there are certain values-civil rights as much as racial equality-that we must preserve at all costs. Up to a point it may be claimed that variations on the democratic theme to suit local conditions are permissible. It may even be argued that, as regards patently deplorable manifestations, the wisest course is to maintain contact in order to exercise such restraining influence as is possible and to encourage the democratic forces that must ultimately prevail. But﻿AUGUST 21, 1964
certainly there is a line beyond which we cannot go in tolerating the membership of governments which deny the few but fundamental principles which have distinguished the commonwealth. These are values of individual liberty and human respect, and how fully we are committed to them is, I think, exemplified by the recent declaration of racial equality made at the prime ministers' meeting in London. Here we see the unique and constructive leadership which the commonwealth can exercise in securing the application under difficult circumstances of democratic principles.
Of course, allowances must be made. It has been said that "people who live differently, think differently". Countries in diverse stages of development cannot possibly subscribe to identical political ideas, still less to identical practices. There are those who wish to see established one all-encompassing institution, covering the commonwealth like an umbrella. There are others who feel that structural formality can only assuage, not cure, internal weakness and dissension. Certainly the idea that disunity among governments can be avoided simply by the creation of international councils is an illusion. At the same time, however, and provided we have a constructive attitude of mind, the innumerable contracts nurtured between our member states over many years, which I have mentioned- governmental, professional, cultural, economic, educational and so on-offer an excellent mechanism for a real contribution to the world order. At their recent meeting, the commonwealth prime ministers conceived of a secretariat that I have no doubt will greatly encourage this function. To quote the communique:
"This secretariat, being recruited from member countries and financed by their contributions, would be at the service of all commonwealth governments and would be a visible symbol of the spirit of co-operation which animates the commonwealth."
Better than talking about the commonwealth is the willingness to use it. Here we have a great conference which exists within the pattern of our relationships, a gathering which reflects a common purpose. No better practical link can be found than in the sphere of education. It was H. G. Wells who said "Human history becomes more and more a race between education and catastrophe". If we accept as an initial proposition that, next to peace, the world's greatest need today is a general lift in the standards of living of the poorer nations, then I think it is obvious that broad educational advance should be our
primary objective. Education must now be regarded as a human right. As such, it is an end in itself, without reference to costs and returns. Its chief purpose is to develop the human personality so that men may take advantage of their spiritual, intellectual and material gifts, to preserve and transmit a society's values and enable people to understand the world in which they live. Only an educational system based on such sound social purposes can develop human resources effectively. Without it, there can be no continuing economic growth, nor can political power be broadly distributed. Undoubtedly, education may cause social tensions since it creates new aspirations and new needs besides opening up fresh opportunities and widening horizons for individuals and nations. It can, however, be the force that also relieves tensions and creates understanding not only within a nation but on an international level as well.
Within the commonwealth, education has always been a common exchange. Even ten years ago more than 50,000 overseas students were receiving instruction in our various countries; the vast majority of them were from other members of our association of nations. Then, less than six years ago, I am happy to say, on Canadian initiative, the commonwealth trade and economic conference at Montreal decided to institute a scheme of scholarships and fellowships. Subsequently, at Oxford and later at New Delhi these plans for straight academic exchange were amplified to include the provision of teachers and teacher-trainers.
If I may inflict some figures upon you, beside the 250 scholars involved in the commonwealth scholarship program, there are some 800 students from the developing countries who are studying or training in Canada under Canadian aid programs and some 160 Canadian educators are serving abroad in commonwealth countries. Since 1950 more than 4,500 scholars and others from the developing countries have received training in Canadian institutions under various Canadian scholarship programs.
Whatever we may think about these programs, it must be admitted that much remains to be done. There are those who say that if we ordinary Canadians knew more about it, we would be inspired to greater efforts. It is true that as recently as 1962 our contributions to these programs of development amounted to only some $60 million per annum, less than 1 per cent of our federal

budget. But about a year ago all this underwent a profound change. It now seems probable that in the fiscal year 1964-1965 upward of $230 million will be available for commitment by Canada to grants, development loans and special credits. Perhaps, as some of our own informed people have said, our attitude is still one of "how much can we spare" instead of "how much can we share", but at least it must be admitted that we are today sparing more freely.
Mr. Lewis Perinbam, until recently secretary general of the Canadian national commission for UNESCO, has pointed out that at present the only centre for commonwealth studies on this continent is to be found at Duke University in North Carolina. He has suggested that, as we approach Canada's centenary, it would be fitting to establish for the use of all our members a Commonwealth study centre in Canada, fully equipped and staffed to perform functions perhaps too obvious to list, and which would be under the aegis of the federal and provincial governments. Perhaps the world's fair building in Montreal might be used to house this Commonwealth study centre.
Of course, Canada's experience is only one example of what is being done about education in the commonwealth. Every country is involved and countless people are now familiar with the problems-the urgent question of the supply of textbooks, for example. But for the newly developing countries the need is frequently for people rather than equipment or money-people with knowledge and experience. We are all in need of more teachers today. Here in Canada we are acutely conscious of this, but our problem is subtly different from that of the less developed countries. We are concerned about automation; about a new way of life which provides all man's wants with little labour and, it seems, at the touch of a button or under the guidance of a computer. Compare this situation with that of some other lands where the most primitive of methods, requiring much labour and a great amount of time, do not produce enough for one man, let alone his family. The problem abroad is to build from the bottom. We are told that in Asia eight million primary school teachers will have to be trained by 1980; this would require
500.000	more teacher-trainers. In Africa, over the same period, the need will amount to
700.000	additional primary school teachers, and, on the educational top level, about
80.000	more members of university staffs.
This third commonwealth education conference is concerned with the vast difficulties involved and the complicated solutions required. We are presented with a frontier giving us abundant opportunities for thought and action. The great heritage of ideas and knowledge which the commonwealth countries offer, can broaden the framework of our co-operation and enrich each member. Aid for education is not really aid at all; it is a form of partnership. Education is a true meeting ground for donor and receiver.
In a sense all nations are "developing" countries. To be economically retarded does not mean culturally backward. If many commonwealth countries are for the moment less advanced than others in economic terms, this cannot dull their great history, rich in cultural and social achievement. We all have something to learn from one another. This is very true of those of us whose origin is European. One recalls the words of Mr. Nehru at the opening of the second conference in 1962;
"European civilization has a magnificent record and yet many people immersed in [it]
.. .had in the past, not so now perhaps, no knowledge of the rest of the world and of the great things the rest of the world has done in the past. It is not a good thing for any cultured and civilized man not to know what has happened elsewhere..."
Through education, reason and observation can be brought to bear on the everyday problems of man's relations with the world and the people about him. Education opens the door of understanding, and besides showing the way to prosperity, lets in the light of peace. These, one need hardly say, are goals worthy of our greatest efforts.
Statement of acceptance of the Chairmanship at the third commonwealth education conference by Honourable Paul Gdrin-Lajoie, Quebec minister of education, Friday August 21, 1964.
Mr. President, Mr. Prime Minister, Mr. Minister for External Affairs, distinguished representatives,
I am deeply impressed by the honour which you have bestowed upon me, in asking me to preside over your work. I do not believe that this honour is offered to me so much in my personal capacity; above all, I see in it a homage to Canada, which I have the honour of representing here with my colleagues from the Canadian delegation, to Quebec, my home province, of which I am

minister of education, and to all my fellow
countrymen.

I wish to see a special meaning in the fact that you chose a minister from a French speaking government to preside over a conference bringing together countries with different languages and cultures, that is true, but where English constitutes a historic bond. Quebec actually forms within the Canadian confederation an homogeneous but different element. Almost a century ago, the two founding races of Canada decided by common agreement to enter into a pact which would enable them to live together while respecting one another's characteristics, language, social and political institutions, and safeguarding also their own interests and aspirations.
English Canada and French Canada are therefore made up, within one country, of both distinctive elements and essential, even integral parts, the union of which has permitted to create, develop and maintain Canada.

Our distinguished president, Right Hon. Vincent Massey, is one of those Canadians who has best understood the profound reality and fundamental importance of Canadian dualism. As an eminent member of the English speaking community, who has to his credit both a highly distinguished public career and many literary accomplishments,
he has acknowledged publicly and in numerous circumstances the essential contribution of his French speaking compatriots to the Canadian identity.
The selection by this conference of a chairman from Quebec also suggests to me a parallel between the commonwealth and Canada; for both today are in their own way primarily dedicated to fostering increased understanding and closer co-operation between partners, while respecting individual particularisms; indeed, it is from this very diversity that the commonwealth today derives its main strength and its purpose, and Canada, its unique personality and character.
I earnestly hope that our exchange of views and the sharing of our varied experiences will make possible a keener appreciation of our solidarity, and that our conference will facilitate an even more active participation of the commonwealth in those tasks for which it is particularly well suited. This accomplishment in turn, while strengthening the bonds which link our governments and peoples, cannot but contribute to greater cooperation and friendship within the whole community of nations.
Because of that sense of equality and of mutual respect inherent in the commonwealth, I know that I can rely on your fullest collaboration toward the success of this conference, particularly since we are all gathered here to seek answers suited to our multiple educational problems. In return, I assure you of my own keenest co-operation in the services of this third commonwealth education conference.
Monday, August 24, 1964
